newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds open stronger on U.S. payrolls data.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds open stronger on U.S. payrolls data.

text.p: Canadian bonds opened much stronger on Friday, boosted by the release of weaker than expected U.S. economic data and some overseas buying, analyst said.
"Those numbers were extremely positive for the market," said Joe Lee, a portfolio manager with Laketon Investment Management. "The psychology was very, very positive going into the number."
Canada's 30-year benchmark bond rose C$0.75 to C$106.00 to yield 7.476 percent against the U.S. 30-year benchmark, which gained 26/32 to yield 6.77 percent.
The spread between the benchmark bonds widened to 71 basis points from 70 basis points at Thursday's close.
North American fixed-income markets rallied this morning after the U.S. Labor Department reported U.S. nonfarm payrolls fell 40,000 in September. Economists had forecast a rise of 166,000.
The data decreased expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will increase interest rates at its next meeting.
"With the Fed probably not moving rates through the rest of 1996 it makes the interest rate forecasts that much more benign for Canada," said one Toronto-based trader.

Dealers said Canadian money markets have now priced in another cut in interest rates by the Bank of Canada even though the central bank cut rates by 25 basis points on Wednesday. Canadian short-term rates are now at their lowest levels since early 1994.
In other prices, the 7.0 percent of 2006 rose C$0.81 to C$101.35 to yield 6.811 percent. The U.S. 10-year benchmark rose 22/32 to yield 6.50 percent.
The spread between the two benchmark bonds narrowed to 31 basis points from 34 basis points at the close of trading on Thursday.
The three-month cash bill traded at 3.48 percent against the U.S. three-month bill at 5.0 percent.
